reference.source: European Association of Neuro-Oncology / EANO-ESMO guidance on leptomeningeal metastasis
clinicalPearls: Suspect leptomeningeal disease when neurological signs are multifocal, involving the cerebral hemispheres, cranial nerves and spinal roots simultaneously in a patient with known cancer.
The commonest solid tumours are breast, lung and melanoma; among haematological malignancies, acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma are typical.
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the whole neuroaxis should precede lumbar puncture and may show leptomeningeal or nerve-root enhancement, subarachnoid nodules or communicating hydrocephalus.
CSF cytology is the diagnostic gold standard but has limited sensitivity on a single sample; large-volume sampling and repeated taps substantially raise the yield.
Typical CSF findings are a raised opening pressure, elevated protein, low glucose and a lymphocytic pleocytosis; flow cytometry is essential when a haematological malignancy is suspected.

Treatment combines intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate, cytarabine, including the liposomal formulation), radiotherapy to symptomatic or bulky sites, and CNS-penetrant systemic or targeted therapy.
An intraventricular reservoir allows more uniform drug distribution than repeated lumbar administration but requires confirmation of unobstructed CSF flow first.
Management is often palliative, prioritising neurological function and symptom control; prognosis is generally measured in weeks to a few months without effective systemic options.
reference.pathophysiology: Tumour cells reach the leptomeninges by haematogenous spread, direct extension from parenchymal or dural deposits, perineural or perivascular migration, or iatrogenic seeding, and then disseminate widely within the cerebrospinal fluid. Coating of the pia-arachnoid and cranial and spinal nerve roots produces the characteristic multifocal deficits, while obstruction of CSF pathways at the arachnoid villi or ventricular outflow causes communicating or obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Competition for glucose and an inflammatory response account for the low CSF glucose and raised protein, and disruption of nerve conduction gives the cranial neuropathies and radiculopathies.
additionalDifferentials: Infective meningitis, including tuberculous and fungal
additionalInvestigations: Gadolinium-enhanced MRI of brain and whole spine
CSF flow cytometry for haematological malignancy
CSF biochemistry with protein and glucose and paired serum glucose
CSF opening pressure at lumbar puncture
CSF tumour markers or circulating tumour DNA where available
Radioisotope CSF flow study before intraventricular therapy
redFlags: Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus
reference.prognosis: Untreated leptomeningeal metastasis progresses rapidly and median survival is short, typically a few weeks to a few months. Outcome is somewhat better where effective, CNS-penetrant systemic therapy exists (for example targetable lung cancer or chemosensitive lymphoma or leukaemia).
pitfalls: Performing lumbar puncture before imaging in a patient with raised intracranial pressure
Accepting a single negative cytology as excluding the diagnosis
Overlooking communicating hydrocephalus as a treatable cause of deterioration
Giving intraventricular therapy without first confirming unobstructed CSF flow
Attributing multifocal neurological signs to a single parenchymal lesion
references: EANO-ESMO clinical practice guidelines on leptomeningeal metastasis from solid tumours
DeVita, Hellman and Rosenberg's Cancer: Principles and Practice of Oncology
management: Treatment intent is mostly palliative, aimed at neurologic function and symptom control, given the setting of advanced systemic disease.
Diagnosis combines neurologic exam, contrast-enhanced MRI of brain and spine, and CSF cytology; up to two repeat CSF exams are recommended if the first is negative due to a high false-negative rate.
If hydrocephalus develops, an external ventricular drain or ventriculoperitoneal shunt should be considered before other CNS-directed treatment.

Radiation therapy palliates symptomatic or bulky sites including cranial neuropathies and cauda equina syndrome; whole-brain radiotherapy is considered for extensive nodular or linear disease or coexisting brain metastases.
Involved-field radiotherapy is often combined with intrathecal chemotherapy and is generally given before intra-CSF therapy due to a neurotoxicity concern with the reverse sequence.
Craniospinal irradiation, historically limited by toxicity, is being reconsidered and may achieve meaningful disease control with acceptable toxicity in selected patients.

Intrathecal chemotherapy (antifolate, antimetabolite, or alkylating agent classes) is the standard approach for leptomeningeal disease without bulky tumor, delivered via an intraventricular reservoir device or lumbar puncture.
An intraventricular device is preferred when CSF flow is not obstructed; bulky meningeal disease impairing CSF flow limits this approach.
Intrathecal HER2-targeted antibody therapy in HER2-positive breast cancer and intrathecal antifolate therapy in EGFR-mutant disease have shown activity but remain limited to early-phase evidence.
Intrathecal chemotherapy after cranial irradiation carries a risk of treatment-related leukoencephalopathy that should be monitored for.
Systemic therapy choice is guided by primary tumor type, prior treatment, and molecular characteristics, since no randomized trial has established a preferred regimen.

CNS-penetrant EGFR-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors show encouraging activity in EGFR-mutant lung cancer with leptomeningeal disease, and CNS-penetrant targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors more broadly may help when a relevant driver mutation is present.

Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy has shown intracranial activity in melanoma and lung cancer brain metastases, though this evidence is drawn from parenchymal brain metastases rather than leptomeningeal disease specifically.

Surgery in this setting is limited to CSF-diversion procedures for hydrocephalus and placement of an intraventricular access device; supportive care (corticosteroids, intracranial pressure and seizure management, symptom palliation) and early multidisciplinary neuro-oncology and palliative care referral are appropriate.
